extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of Rabelais / Renaissance satire; general readers of classic literature
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and maxims embedded in a satirical legal narrative (Rabelais' description of judges, procedures, and reasoning). The chunk foregrounds mock-legal standards, procedural rationales, and pragmatic maxims guiding judicial behaviour in the tale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfections of nature are not crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: The imperfections of nature should never be imputed unto any for crimes and transgressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an excuse for mistakes arising from infirmity (e.g., old age, dim sight); invoked to obtain a favourable opinion of uprightness despite procedural prevarication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of chance/dice (Alea Judiciorum) to decide suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Chance and fortune are good, honest, profitable, and necessary for ending of and putting a final closure to dissensions and debates in suits at law (Alea Judiciorum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an established doctrine with citations; used to justify awarding judgments by lot when matters are obscure or to bring finality to disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the custom and rules of the judicatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct and regulate actions and procedures according to the custom of the judicatory and the rule thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge's practice should conform to established doctrine and customary procedure ('my practice is therein the same with that of your other worships'). Custom legitimizes otherwise odd practices (like deciding by dice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve formalities even if substance suffers
rubrics_metrics.description: The omission of formalities maketh all, whatever is done, to be of no force nor value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalities are necessary for validity; legal proceedings require formal documents and steps even when they may 'utterly destroy the materialities and substances' of causes—thus formality is prioritized as a rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use degree of randomness appropriate to the case (small vs large dice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ small dice when there are many bags (complex/obscure matters) and large dice when the matter is plain and there are fewer bags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A humorous ‘rule’ about scaling the randomness: 'Semper in obscuris quod minimum est sequimur' — in obscure matters follow the smallest option; choose the instrument of chance to match the complexity/number of filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award judgment to the party who wins the lot
rubrics_metrics.description: Give out sentence in his favour unto whom hath befallen the best chance by dice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When resorting to lottery/lot, the judicial pronouncement follows the outcome of the chance; this enacts finality and distributes consequences according to the lot ('Qui prior est tempore potior est jure' and other maxims are cited alongside).

rubrics_metrics.name: Documents/filings serve three roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Writings and papers serve (1) for formality (without which actions are void), (2) as a healthful exercise/recreation for judges, and (3) as means to allow truth to ripen with time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative lists these three uses explicitly: formal necessity; recreational/stimulating occupation (preventing ill-health from lack of exercise); and aiding maturation of the cause by providing material that time will process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay/protraction to allow time to ripen truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Defer, protract, delay, prolong... the time of giving a definitive sentence, that the suit... may come at last to its full ripeness and maturity. Time is the father of truth and virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postponement is justified so matters can be 'fanned and winnowed' and parties will bear adverse outcomes more patiently; analogous to waiting for fruit or a disease to reach crisis before acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervene later when parties are exhausted (timing of mediation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take disputes at their decadence/when parties are weary and their purses emptied to secure reconciliation; reconciliers obtain agreement best when parties are 'weaning' or drained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediator tactic: do not try to reconcile at the outbreak of dispute; wait until litigants have spent resources and their heat of contest abates—then a mediator can obtain accords more easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow suits to mature via accumulation of procedural acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A suit at its first beginning is shapeless and imperfect; when heaps of papers are packed and put up in bags, the suit becomes well-formed and complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigation gains 'form' and legitimacy through successive filings, reports, and formal acts; the growth of procedural trappings is depicted as constitutive of the action's identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pauses and sleep to pacify tempers and avoid hasty action
rubrics_metrics.description: Permit the plaintiff to depart and sleep, require attestation of that sleep, then convene him; sleep often pacifies anger and prevents imprudent fights: 'Quandoque bonus dormitat Homerus.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comic procedural rule: inserting enforced pauses (and rituals proving repose) is a means to calm passions so that violent or hasty decisions do not ensue; illustrated by story of sleeping combatants who reconcile after rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider long prior good service and character in mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A single fault should be swallowed up by the immense ocean of just dooms and sentences which heretofore he hath given; old age and simplicity warrant excuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or pardoning, take account of a judge's long record of upright sentences and personal qualities (old age, simplicity) as grounds for mercy or mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: In obscurity, favour the defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: Quum sunt partium jura obscura, reo potius favendum est quam actori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parties' rights are obscure, the rule (as cited) is to favor the accused/defendant rather than the plaintiff/actor; invoked as a legal maxim justifying leniency in doubtful cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal priority gives stronger legal right
rubrics_metrics.description: Qui prior est tempore potior est jure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where timing matters, the party earlier in time has the stronger claim in law; cited among other maxims that structure adjudicative outcomes.
